title: 3-Read Friday #105: NPPPN Sequence, the Do Now, and the AI Death Zone
author: Craig Barton
summary: 3-Read Friday #105 opens with a joint post from Dario Emanuele and Peter, showing that the NPPPN sequence structure -- rooted in Engelmann and Carnine's work -- helps students build robust concept understanding by presenting carefully varied positive and negative examples one at a time. Dylan Kane then argues that an effective Do Now routine should be deliberately simple: short, retrieval-focused, and easy to prepare, because the start of a lesson is the hardest time in the day to teach well. The issue closes with Chris Wheadon's 'AI Death Zone,' a cautionary counterpoint to Barton's own earlier post on the democratisation of resource creation, warning about the risks of AI-generated teaching materials. Barton frames the Wheadon piece as a genuine point of internal tension for him, noting it argues against sentiments in his own prior writing.
points: The NPPPN sequence (rooted in Engelmann and Carnine) builds robust concept understanding by presenting carefully varied positive and negative examples one at a time, rather than en masse.
Kane's Do Now principle: deliberate simplicity -- short, retrieval-focused, low-prep -- beats elaborate routines, because lesson openings are the hardest moment in the day to teach well.

Wheadon's 'AI Death Zone' is a direct counter-argument to the trend of AI-empowered bespoke resource creation that Barton himself has praised, warning of real downside risk in unchecked AI-generated materials.
Barton explicitly flags his own uncertainty here, inviting readers to weigh Wheadon's caution against his own more optimistic prior take on AI-assisted resource creation.
